meta.title: Bicycles and the jungle myth — Malaya 1941-42 (living-library test)

scenes.beat: The Japanese army also came with a very practical idea.
It did not bring many bicycles.
It knew Malaya was full of them,
so it took them from shops and civilians
and rode south.
A British officer who lay hidden beside a road behind the Japanese lines
later described them cycling past in groups of 40 or 50, 3 or 4 abreast,
chatting and laughing as if they were off to a football match,
which brings us to the first myth at the gate, the jungle.
You'll often hear that the British thought Malaya's jungle was passable,
so the Japanese simply walked through it.
The truth is more awkward.
Much of what everyone called jungle was actually rubber plantations,
coconut groves, villages, and roads.

scenes.tag: The edge of the jungle, Malaya
scenes.beat: The real jungle at the edges looked impenetrable,
and the Australian official history says that impression was misleading.

scenes.tag: The edge of the jungle, Malaya
scenes.beat: The Japanese mostly didn't hack through Virgin Forest.
They used the roads and the plantations,
went around the British positions on the paths beside them,
and kept moving faster than the defenders could dig in.
